setup: Stand upright with your feet hip-width apart and knees soft.
Hold a dumbbell in one hand at your side with an arm hanging straight and a neutral grip.
Place your free hand behind your head or resting on your opposite hip.
steps: Keeping your hips square and shoulders facing forward, slowly bend your torso laterally toward the weighted side until you feel a gentle stretch in the opposite flank.
Contract the obliques on the unweighted side to pull your torso smoothly back to the upright position.
Optionally continue slightly past vertical into a modest lateral contraction, then return to center under control.
Complete all repetitions on one side before switching the dumbbell to the opposite hand.
instructions.breathing: Inhale as you laterally lower the weight down the side of your thigh, and exhale as you contract your obliques to return upright.
cues: Bend directly sideways without leaning forward or twisting.
Move strictly from the spine while keeping your pelvis stationary.
Pull with your opposite waist to stand tall.

common_faults.fault: Holding dumbbells in both hands simultaneously, which creates a counterbalance and eliminates tension on the target muscles.
common_faults.correction: Hold only one dumbbell at a time so your lateral core must work against an asymmetrical load.

common_faults.fault: Rotating the hips or flexing forward at the waist during the bend.
common_faults.correction: Move strictly within the frontal plane as if sliding your back along a flat wall.

common_faults.fault: Using excessive momentum or over-bending past an active, pain-free range of motion.
common_faults.correction: Use a controlled tempo and lower the dumbbell only as far as comfortable lateral spinal flexion allows.

precautions: Avoid aggressive overbending or bouncing at the bottom of the movement to protect the lumbar spine.

name: Dumbbell Side Bend
summary: A standing lateral trunk exercise targeting the obliques and quadratus lumborum by flexing and extending the spine laterally against single-sided resistance.
